claim: The Weighted Normal modifier only fixes shading distortion on FLAT-surface bevel geometry (where holding-edge angles aren't exactly the intended value, e.g. slightly-off-90-degree corners) -- it does NOT fix shading distortion on curved surfaces, because that is a different underlying problem: a genuinely bent/non-planar polygon face, not a normal-weighting issue.
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript, 2026-08-15): 'if I add a weighted normal, this will not fix the problem. And that's because this is not a flat surface. This is a curved surface, which has a completely different problem altogether... This has nothing to do with weighted normals. That won't fix the problem.' Demonstrated by duplicating and separating a single bent quad face out of a curved-surface boolean result to show it is literally non-planar.
rejected_alternative: Assuming Weighted Normal is a general-purpose fix for any post-boolean/post-bevel shading distortion, and reaching for it on a curved-surface asset (like the teapot body/spout, a cylindrical shackle, or any revolved form) the way it might be reached for on a flat panel.
reason: This is a real, concrete boundary condition on this project's existing bevel-weight/Weighted-Normal policy (from the Level 16 manual study: 'Face Strength + Weighted Normal Face Influence is a winner-take-all mechanism') that hasn't been stated anywhere in this project's docs yet. Every hard-surface asset built so far (teapot, door handle, stapler attempt) has curved surfaces, so this boundary is directly load-bearing, not a hypothetical edge case.

claim: For shading distortion on a genuinely curved surface (not fixable by Weighted Normal), the three fixes in order of practicality are: (1) clean quad-based topology from the start, so no face is ever left bent; (2) denser support geometry, which isolates the unavoidable distortion into small ngons/triangles that are visually negligible even though technically still present -- described as 'the way I've always taught with a hard surface modeling workflow'; (3) a Data Transfer modifier pulling custom split normals from a clean duplicate, described as real but 'not as practical.'
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript): 'there's really only two ways to fix it. Three ways actually. The first one is to have good topology to begin with... The second way here, and the way I've always taught with a hard surface modeling workflow, is to simply have more geometry to isolate the shading... the third way you can fix it, which isn't as practical, is with a data transfer modifier.'
rejected_alternative: Reaching for a Weighted Normal modifier on curved-surface shading distortion (see the PRINCIPLE item above) or leaving the distortion unaddressed because a bevel-weight/weighted-normal pass didn't visibly help.
reason: A ranked, practical decision tree for curved-surface shading defects -- directly actionable the next time a curved hard-surface part (teapot body, any future cylindrical part) shows post-boolean or post-bevel shading artifacts that a Weighted Normal modifier doesn't resolve.

claim: A Mark Sharp edge, when the edge it's on later gets beveled, splits into TWO 'holding edges' (one on each side of the new bevel strip) that both inherit the sharp marking -- producing a visible unwanted seam line running along the bevel. Three fixes: clear Mark Sharp on both holding edges after beveling; clear Mark Sharp BEFORE beveling in the first place (avoids the problem entirely); or, in HardOps specifically, use its 'recalculate' feature (Ctrl+Shift+click) to reassign sharp markings based on the mesh's current angles rather than manually hunting for the stale marking.
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript): 'whenever I bevel that, this edge right here splits into two holding edges, one right here on the bevel and then one right here on the bevel. It splits that edge into two holding edges, which is going to hold... that sharp marking. So, there's two ways to fix this, three ways to fix this.'
rejected_alternative: Treating a stray sharp-edge seam line on a bevel as an unexplained shading bug and trying to fix it via smooth-angle threshold tweaking, which doesn't address the actual cause (a stale Mark Sharp inherited by the bevel's holding edges).
reason: A specific, previously-undocumented failure mode for this project's Mark Sharp / bevel-weight combination -- relevant any time an edge is marked sharp before a Bevel modifier or bevel_selection op is later applied to it or an adjacent edge.

claim: Manual Mark Sharp exists specifically for the case where Auto Smooth's single angle threshold cannot correctly separate a shallow/steep boolean-created edge from its neighbors without also wrongly flattening unrelated nearby geometry -- i.e. it's an escape hatch for when angle-based auto-smoothing genuinely cannot express the desired sharp/smooth boundary, not a general substitute for angle-based smoothing.
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript): 'the main reason this feature even exists in Blender is for situations where the auto smooth doesn't capture the angle as you want'; demonstrated with a boolean cut at a shallow angle where adjusting the auto-smooth angle to capture the new edge also incorrectly flattens an unrelated area.
rejected_alternative: Treating Mark Sharp as a general-purpose alternative to Smooth-by-Angle rather than a targeted fix for angle-threshold conflicts specifically.
reason: Clarifies WHEN to reach for Mark Sharp within this project's existing set_smooth_by_angle-based shading policy -- as a scoped override for cases the single global angle threshold can't resolve, not as a first-choice tool.
